lead: A doped semiconductor has far more electrons than holes, or the reverse. The dopant density decides which, and by how much. Fermi-Dirac statistics fixes the rest: the minority density, the Fermi level position, and how both move with temperature. Every diode, transistor, LED and solar cell depends on this balance.
prereq: You need 7.2 Fermi-Dirac statistics and the Fermi energy and 7.3 energy bands and the intrinsic carrier concentration n_i.

sections.h3: Carrier density from the Fermi level

blocks.text: A phosphorus atom in silicon donates one electron bound by about 45 meV. At room temperature most of these electrons reach the conduction band. Counting them is Fermi-Dirac book-keeping.

blocks.where: n is the electron concentration (m⁻³ or cm⁻³); N_C is the effective density of states at the conduction band edge, in the same unit; E_C is the conduction band edge energy in eV; E_F is the Fermi energy in eV; k_B = 8.617×10⁻⁵ eV/K (1.381×10⁻²³ J/K) is the Boltzmann constant, so k_BT comes out in eV; T is the temperature in kelvin. At 300 K, k_BT = 0.0259 eV.

p is the hole concentration; N_V is the effective density of states at the valence band edge; E_V is the valence band edge energy in eV. A hole is an empty state, so the further E_F sits above E_V, the fewer holes there are.

blocks.text: N_C and N_V come from the band curvature, that is, from the effective masses.

blocks.where: m_e* is the electron effective mass near the band edge; h = 6.626×10⁻³⁴ J s is the Planck constant. N_V uses the hole effective mass m_h* in the same expression. For silicon at 300 K, N_C ≈ 2.8×10¹⁹ cm⁻³ and N_V ≈ 1.0×10¹⁹ cm⁻³.

blocks.text: Both formulas are the Boltzmann tail of f(E) = 1/(1 + exp[(E − E_F)/k_BT]). Once E − E_F exceeds about 3k_BT the 1 drops out and f(E) ≈ exp[−(E − E_F)/k_BT]. Multiply that tail by the number of available states to get the carrier formulas. This non-degenerate case covers the whole chapter.

items: Raising T at fixed E_F raises both n and p, because the tails reach further into the bands.
Raising E_F raises n and lowers p: the Fermi level is the knob.
Doping moves E_F; that is the whole mechanism of an extrinsic semiconductor.

sections.h3: Mass action, charge neutrality, and the doping answer

blocks.text: Two relations tie the four quantities together. The first is the law of mass action, from multiplying the two carrier formulas with E_g = E_C − E_V.
n p = n_i²,   n_i² = N_C N_V exp(−E_g/k_BT)
blocks.where: n_i is the intrinsic carrier concentration, about 1.0×10¹⁰ cm⁻³ for silicon at 300 K; E_g = E_C − E_V is the band gap, 1.12 eV for silicon. The product n p depends only on temperature and material, never on doping.

blocks.text: The second is charge neutrality: a piece of semiconductor carries no net charge, so mobile electrons plus negative acceptor ions balance holes plus positive donor ions.

blocks.where: N_D⁺ is the ionised donor concentration (positive, the donors gave up electrons) and N_A⁻ the ionised acceptor concentration (negative), both in cm⁻³. At room temperature assume full ionisation: N_D⁺ = N_D and N_A⁻ = N_A.

items: n-type, no acceptors: N_A = 0, so charge neutrality reads n = N_D + p.
N_D far exceeds n_i, so p is negligible and the majority density is n ≈ N_D.
Mass action then gives the minority density p = n_i²/N_D.
Invert n = N_C exp[−(E_C − E_F)/k_BT] with n = N_D: E_C − E_F = k_BT ln(N_C/N_D).
p-type: swap donors and acceptors to get p ≈ N_A, n ≈ n_i²/N_A and E_F − E_V = k_BT ln(N_V/N_A).

blocks.text: E_C − E_F is positive in n-type material: the Fermi level sits k_BT ln(N_C/N_D) below the conduction band edge, a few tenths of an eV in silicon — about 0.2 eV at N_D = 10¹⁶ cm⁻³, several k_BT. In p-type material E_F sits above E_V by k_BT ln(N_V/N_A). Heavier doping pushes the Fermi level closer to the band.

sections.h3: How carrier density changes with temperature

blocks.text: A doped crystal passes through three regimes as it warms.

items: Freeze-out, very low temperature. k_BT is far below the donor binding energy (about 45 meV for phosphorus in silicon), so electrons stay bound and n falls as T falls. For silicon this ends near 50 K.
Extrinsic, the working range. Every donor is ionised, n ≈ N_D stays roughly constant, while p = n_i²/N_D rises slowly. The Fermi level is locked at E_C − k_BT ln(N_C/N_D). Most devices live here.
Intrinsic, high temperature. n_i grows as T^(3/2) exp(−E_g/2k_BT) and eventually reaches N_D; past that n ≈ p ≈ n_i and E_F drifts back to mid-gap.

blocks.text: The flat middle region exists only because N_D far exceeds n_i. When the two are comparable, n ≈ N_D fails.

blocks.where: This is the exact solution of n = N_D + n_i²/n, with p = n_i²/n to follow. It assumes full ionisation: when n_i << N_D (extrinsic range) n → N_D, and when n_i >> N_D (intrinsic range) n → n_i. Below the freeze-out temperature the donors are not fully ionised and this formula no longer applies.

blocks.text: One limit: when N_D approaches N_C (about 2.8×10¹⁹ cm⁻³ for silicon), E_F enters the conduction band, the Boltzmann tail fails and the full Fermi-Dirac function is needed. That is degenerate doping, and this chapter stays below it.

figure.caption: Doping branches into a donor route and an acceptor route. The donor route fixes n ≈ N_D, the acceptor route fixes p ≈ N_A; both meet at mass action, which supplies the minority carrier.

spec.title: Doping sets carrier density
spec.aria: Doping branches into donor and acceptor paths, giving n-type and p-type carrier densities that meet at the mass-action relation.

examples.question: A silicon sample at 300 K has donors only, N_D = 1.0×10¹⁶ cm⁻³, with N_C = 2.8×10¹⁹ cm⁻³, n_i = 1.0×10¹⁰ cm⁻³ and k_BT = 0.0259 eV. Assuming full ionisation, find n, p and E_C − E_F.
steps: N_D is a million times n_i, so the sample is firmly extrinsic at 300 K.
Charge neutrality gives n = N_D + p with p negligible, so n ≈ N_D = 1.0×10¹⁶ cm⁻³.
0.21 eV exceeds 3k_BT = 0.078 eV, so the non-degenerate formula holds, and the level lies inside the 1.12 eV gap.
examples.answer: n ≈ 1.0×10¹⁶ cm⁻³, p ≈ 1.0×10⁴ cm⁻³, and E_C − E_F ≈ 0.21 eV, so the Fermi level lies 0.21 eV below the conduction band edge.
examples.check:
import math
N_D = 1.0e16
N_C = 2.8e19
n_i = 1.0e10
k_BT = 0.0259
n = N_D
p = n_i * n_i / n
E_C_minus_E_F = k_BT * math.log(N_C / n)
print(n)
print(p)
print(round(E_C_minus_E_F, 2))

traps: Writing n = N_D when N_D is close to n_i, or at high temperature. Use n = (N_D + √(N_D² + 4n_i²))/2 there.
Mixing cm⁻³ and m⁻³: 1 m⁻³ is 10⁻⁶ cm⁻³, a factor of a million. Silicon data come in cm⁻³.
Sign slips in the Fermi level. In n-type material E_C − E_F is small and positive; in p-type the small quantity is E_F − E_V. E_F − E_C would be negative.
Treating n p = n_i² as always true. It holds in thermal equilibrium only; under illumination or forward injection the product exceeds n_i².
Calling N_C the number of electrons. N_C is the number of available states per unit volume at the band edge; the exponential decides how many are occupied.

quiz.q: Define the effective density of states N_C and give its value for silicon at 300 K.
quiz.a: N_C = 2(2π m_e* k_BT/h²)^(3/2) is the number of available states per unit volume at the conduction band edge, with m_e* the electron effective mass. For silicon at 300 K, N_C ≈ 2.8×10¹⁹ cm⁻³.

quiz.q: State the law of mass action for a semiconductor in thermal equilibrium.
quiz.a: n p = n_i², where n and p are the electron and hole concentrations and n_i is the intrinsic concentration. The product is fixed by temperature and band gap, not by doping.

quiz.q: Why does adding donors move the Fermi level towards the conduction band?
quiz.a: n = N_C exp[−(E_C − E_F)/k_BT] can hold a larger n only if E_C − E_F shrinks, so E_F moves up towards E_C. Acceptors do the reverse, moving E_F down towards E_V.

quiz.q: Silicon at 300 K has N_D = 4.0×10¹⁶ cm⁻³, N_C = 2.8×10¹⁹ cm⁻³, n_i = 1.0×10¹⁰ cm⁻³ and k_BT = 0.0259 eV. Find p and E_C − E_F.
A p-type silicon sample has N_A = 5.0×10¹⁵ cm⁻³, N_V = 1.0×10¹⁹ cm⁻³, n_i = 1.0×10¹⁰ cm⁻³ at 300 K. Find E_F − E_V and the electron concentration.
Sketch log n against 1/T for an n-type sample and explain the slope in each of the three regions.
quiz.a: Low T: steep fall with slope −E_d/(2k_B), where E_d is the donor ionisation energy — freeze-out. Middle: a flat plateau, n ≈ N_D. High T: a rise with slope −E_g/(2k_B), because n → n_i ∝ exp(−E_g/2k_BT) — the intrinsic region. The plateau is widest when N_D is many orders of magnitude above n_i.

quiz.q: Explain why n ≈ N_D stops being valid at high temperature, and what replaces it.
quiz.a: The approximation dropped p from n = N_D + p, and p = n_i²/n grows fast with T. When n_i becomes comparable to N_D it cannot be dropped. Solving the quadratic gives n = (N_D + √(N_D² + 4n_i²))/2, which tends to N_D when n_i is small and to n_i when n_i is large.

beyond: Not for the exam. Push the doping past about 10¹⁹ cm⁻³ and the Fermi level enters the band; the Boltzmann tail fails and the material becomes a degenerate semiconductor, halfway to a metal. Heavily doped indium tin oxide films are both transparent and conducting, which is why they coat touch screens and solar cell tops. MOSFET source and drain regions are doped degenerately on purpose, to make thin tunnel barriers. A Hall effect measurement is the standard way to extract n or p and the mobility together. Useful search terms: degenerate semiconductor, Mott transition, Hall coefficient.
